title: The Borrowed Confession
premise: Yara Thornbury, the coroner of the fading mill town of Harrow's Bend, signs off on the death of local patriarch Edmund Voss as a heart attack—until an anonymous confession arrives, postmarked the day after the funeral, claiming Voss was poisoned and daring her to prove it. As Yara quietly reopens the file, more letters arrive, each revealing details only the killer or someone with access to the original investigation could know, and she realizes her late mentor's old case notes were stolen from her own office. The letters are bait in a game of justice outside the law: the writer, Voss's estranged daughter posing as her own family's hired archivist, is punishing the town's powerful men who covered up a death decades ago, and she intends to make Yara—whose signature once closed that old case—her final accomplice. In the end, Yara must choose between exposing a killer whose victims were themselves murderers, or letting the confession's last letter, addressed to her by name, decide her identity for her.
about_author: Jude Underhill is the pen name of a former rural records clerk who spent a decade cataloguing small-town deaths, wills, and disappearances before turning to fiction. They write from a farmhouse in the northern hills, where the nearest neighbor is a cemetery.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She signs the death certificate for Edmund Voss, the town's richest man, and reflects on the graves she knows like neighbors. A quiet, competent opening that establishes her invisibility and her habit of speaking to the dead. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Two days after the funeral, a letter arrives claiming Voss was poisoned with digitalis, dated the day he was buried. The handwriting is elegant, the details precise—too precise. Yara tells no one. Emotional beat: the first crack in her ordered world.

chapters.title: What the Body Keeps
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She exhumed nothing—she can't—but she pulls Voss's bloodwork from the hospital and finds an anomaly a doctor waved away. Deputy Callum Reyes notices her digging. Emotional beat: the thrill of competence curdling into fear.

chapters.title: The Archivist
chapters.summary: New character POV: Vera Voss, Edmund's estranged daughter, arrives in town posing as an archivist hired to organize the estate. She watches Yara with unsettling attention. Readers suspect her; Yara does not. Emotional beat: dramatic irony tightening like wire.

chapters.title: A Second Letter
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Another letter arrives—this one about a different man, Councilman Breck, who is suddenly, conveniently ill. The writer knows details of a case file Yara closed eleven years ago. She checks her office: her mentor's old notes are missing. Emotional beat: violation.

chapters.title: The Town That Looks Away
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. He investigates Voss's death officially and finds the town's elite closing ranks—lawyers, the bank president, the doctor who signed the certificate. Flashbacks hint at a drowning in 1989 that everyone remembers differently. Emotional beat: the rot beneath respectability.

chapters.title: Grave Knowledge
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She visits the 1989 grave—a boy named Danny Ferro, ruled accidental drowning—and admits to herself her own signature on that old file was a kindness to her dying mentor, not the truth. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing like a body in spring thaw.

chapters.title: The Third Letter
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The letters now name their pattern: three men who were boys together in 1989. Breck dies. The letter arrives postmarked the day of his funeral. Yara realizes the writer is timing confessions to funerals—performing justice as ritual. Emotional beat: horror at the elegance.

chapters.title: Suspects and Shadows
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. He suspects Yara herself—the letters reference details only she had. Their alliance frays. Meanwhile Vera offers Yara help cataloguing the Voss estate, getting closer to the coroner's office. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; trust becoming a liability.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Confession
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She confronts Dr. Pell, the third target and the man who certified both deaths. He nearly confesses to the 1989 cover-up, then is found dead before he can sign a statement. Yara arrived too late—by minutes. Emotional beat: the killer is always one step ahead.

chapters.title: Ink and Ash
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Forensics on the letters: paper from the Voss estate, ink matching an archival fountain pen. The killer has access to the estate—and to the coroner's old files. Callum quietly puts surveillance on both Vera and Yara. Emotional beat: the net closing on the wrong people.

chapters.title: What Yara Signed
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A letter arrives addressed to her by name, quoting her own eleven-year-old case note verbatim: 'closed as accidental, with regret.' The writer knows she falsified nothing but signed anyway. Emotional beat: being seen—utterly—for the first time in years.

chapters.title: The Ferro File
chapters.summary: Vera's POV (unlabeled, revealed as such). She reconstructs 1989: her brother Danny, the four boys on the mill bridge, the pact of silence bought by the Voss name. Her father's death was the first payment. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into purpose.

chapters.title: An Offer in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Vera, mask slipping, proposes a partnership: Yara's access, Vera's evidence, and the town's reckoning—outside the law, because the law already failed once. Yara refuses, but doesn't report her. Emotional beat: the seduction of complicity.

chapters.title: The Fourth Letter
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A letter arrives that isn't a confession—it's a threat, warning Vera off, written in a different hand. There is a second player: someone in the old cover-up protecting themselves. The bank president, Aldous Crane. Emotional beat: the game has more pieces than she thought.

chapters.title: Crane's Ledger
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. He finds Crane's payments to the doctor, the sheriff of 1989, and Yara's late mentor—a pension for silence. The mentor Yara loved was bought. Emotional beat: betrayal of the dead, and of her own memory of him.

chapters.title: Night at the Estate
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She breaks into the Voss estate to find the original 1989 evidence Vera claims to hold. She finds Vera drugged and the archive burning—Crane got there first. Yara saves Vera and one scorched box of files. Emotional beat: choosing a side with her hands.

chapters.title: Two Confessions
chapters.summary: Alternating Yara/Vera. In a safehouse, Vera confesses the killings; Yara confesses the signature. They read the salvaged files together and find Crane's name in Danny's own handwriting—a note the boy mailed the day he died. Emotional beat: two kinds of guilt finding common ground.

chapters.title: The Trap
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Yara turns herself in for the old falsification to force the case open, trading her testimony for a sting: a fake fifth letter luring Crane to destroy the last evidence. Emotional beat: sacrifice as strategy; the coroner makes herself the body on the table.

chapters.title: Reckoning at the Bridge
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Crane comes to the mill bridge to burn the final file and finish Vera. Confrontation in the dark; Callum's team closes in; Crane, cornered, nearly forces Yara off the bridge where Danny died. Vera's testimony and the salvaged files convict him. Emotional beat: the past literally trying to repeat itself, and failing.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. From jail, Vera sends one final letter: no confession, just the question of whether justice done wrongly is still justice—and Yara's own signature as the answer. Yara faces suspension, maybe charges. Emotional beat: the cost made personal.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She keeps her job by a thread—or loses it, by choice—and adds a stone to Danny Ferro's grave with his real name and the word 'brother.' The town begins, uneasily, to tell the truth. Emotional beat: quiet, hard-won peace; identity no longer borrowed.
